analysis.one_liner: Bans rental companies from renting or selling vehicles under a safety recall before the defect is fixed.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it was referred to two committees and their subcommittees in May 2015 and saw no further action before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already barred car dealers from selling new vehicles that are under a safety recall, but it left a gap for rental companies: a rental fleet could keep handing customers a car that the manufacturer had recalled as unsafe. This bill, named for two sisters who died in a rented car with a known steering defect, would have required rental companies to stop renting or selling a recalled vehicle within 24 hours of getting the manufacturer's notice (48 hours for large fleets), unless a temporary fix in the notice made it safe. It would also have let the Transportation Secretary inspect rental companies' records during safety investigations, required a study of rental truck recall repairs, and explicitly protected manufacturers from any new liability under the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of car rental companies, who today can be handed a vehicle the manufacturer has recalled for a safety defect. It also protects anyone who later buys an ex-rental car that would previously have been sold while still recalled, since the bill bans both renting and selling recalled fleet vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car rental customers and used-car buyers

how_it_helps.text: Requires a rental company to stop selling, leasing, or renting a recalled vehicle as soon as practicable, and no later than 24 hours after receiving the manufacturer's defect notice — or 48 hours when the notice covers more than 5,000 vehicles in its fleet [S2] [S3].

Closes a gap in existing law: the underlying statute's dealer protections are extended to rental companies, so a recalled vehicle in a rental fleet gets the same treatment as one on a dealer's lot [S3].

Lets a company keep renting a recalled vehicle only if the manufacturer's notice specifies a temporary alteration that eliminates the safety risk, and it must stop renting once the real repair becomes available [S2] [S3].

Bars rental companies from disabling safety devices on vehicles, and gives the Transportation Secretary authority to inspect rental companies' records and require reports during safety investigations — powers previously limited to dealers [S2] [S3].
Adds a mandatory seven-year evaluation of whether safety recall remedies are being completed on rental trucks, with a report and legislative recommendations to Congress [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rental car companies, which would have to track recall notices, pull recalled vehicles from their fleets within a day, and absorb the cost of parking unrepaired cars until fixed — costs that could be partly passed to renters through prices. Automakers would face faster pull-through of recall repairs by fleets but gain an explicit statement that the bill creates no new or increased liability for them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Car rental companies and fleet operators

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly states it creates no new or increased liability for manufacturers of recalled vehicles and leaves existing manufacturer–rental company contracts untouched, so automakers bear none of the added enforcement burden the bill creates [S2] [S3].
It applies only to larger operations: a 'rental company' must run a fleet of five or more rental vehicles, so very small rental businesses fall outside the rules [S3].

Rental companies would face real compliance and downtime costs — recalled vehicles sit unrented until repaired — and industry compliance expenses are typically recovered through rental prices, so renters could pay somewhat more per day in exchange for the safety guarantee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: a renter can no longer be handed a car the manufacturer has formally recalled as unsafe, and the repair happens sooner because fleets can't keep unsafe vehicles in circulation. The costs are one-sided in the bill's design — the rental industry bears compliance costs and manufacturers get an explicit liability shield — but that shield was the political price of extending dealer rules to fleets, and it does not weaken the core 24-hour pull rule. The main honest criticism is the fleet-size floor of five vehicles, which leaves small operators unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure committees on the day it was introduced, bounced to two subcommittees three days later, and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the bill on May 1, 2015, joined by Reps. G.K. Butterfield, Walter Jones, and Jan Schakowsky [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee for provisions in their jurisdictions [S5].
Within days it was referred to the Highways and Transit subcommittee (May 4) and the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittee (May 8) [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no committee vote, no House floor vote, and no Senate companion action is recorded before the 114th Congress expired on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Car rental companies, which for the remainder of the Congress faced no federal requirement to pull recalled vehicles from their fleets within a day, and manufacturers, who keep the status quo in which the rental gap is unregulated.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — three cosponsors, two Democrats and one Republican (Walter Jones of North Carolina) — and no vote was ever taken, so the bill's support never got a partisan test on the floor.

industries.industry: Car rental companies (Hertz, Enterprise, Avis and other large fleet operators)
industries.note: The bill forces fleets to stop renting and selling recalled vehicles within 24–48 hours of a defect notice and opens their records to safety investigators, a direct cost to their business model of keeping cars in revenue service. Because that cost exists to keep their customers from driving recalled cars, the industry's interest here runs against its own bottom line and with renters.

Faster fleet compliance accelerates recall repair completion, which automakers must pay for, but the bill explicitly creates or increases no manufacturer liability and preserves existing manufacturer–rental company contracts. Their role in the recall system is unchanged rather than entrenched.

The bill mandates a seven-year federal study of whether recall repairs are completed on rental trucks and a report with legislative recommendations, adding scrutiny but no immediate requirements. The scrutiny could later lead to rules covering rental trucks, which are currently outside the bill's 10,000-pound coverage ceiling.
